passage: On the first cold morning of December, the anganwadi floor is covered with a warm durrie, and the red truck is the best toy. Mridul, five, has it. Vishal comes over. Yesterday Vishal let Mridul hold his clay elephant. "Here," says Mridul, and pushes the truck across. Then Bunty holds out his hand. Bunty never shares his crayons, not even the broken ones. Mridul pulls the truck back to his chest. "No. You didn't give me yesterday." Bunty's lip trembles. The didi kneels down. "Hmm. What could Bunty do?" Bunty looks at his crayons.

qa.q: What did Vishal let Mridul hold yesterday?
qa.a: His clay elephant.

qa.q: Why does Mridul pull the truck back when Bunty asks?
qa.a: He feels it isn't fair and is a bit cross that Bunty never shares his crayons, so he only gives to the friend who gave to him.

qa.q: How does the didi handle it, and why is that a good idea?
qa.a: She asks what Bunty could do, helping the children see that sharing goes both ways without scolding anyone 🙂.

qa.q: What is it like for Bunty to be refused?
qa.a: Bunty feels hurt and close to tears, and starts to look at his own crayons in a new way.

grounding: A young child shares a toy with the friend who shared yesterday and refuses the one who never shares.

passage: Last Eid, when I was nine, I kept a list in my head all day. Simran had carried the plates. I had stirred the seviyan. Our cousin Ayaan had done nothing except eat raisins. When Khala handed out the nankhatai biscuits, she gave me five and Simran three, because I'd been in the kitchen longest. I should have been happy. Instead I shouted, "That's not FAIR! Four and four!" Everyone stared. Khala laughed. "Zainab, you're complaining about getting MORE?" I was. It felt wrong in my tummy. Then I told Khala that Ayaan should get only one because he did nothing, and nobody laughed at that. Now I think fair is a bit more wobbly than I thought.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Khala give Simran?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Zainab shout "That's not FAIR" about getting more?
qa.a: Zainab felt uncomfortable and upset, with a wrong feeling in the tummy, because an unequal split seemed unfair even with the extra coming to Zainab.

qa.q: What could Khala say to help Zainab think about fairness?
qa.a: Khala could praise Zainab's care for fairness and talk gently about how sharing can be kind, not only exact, so Ayaan isn't cut down to one biscuit.

qa.q: How might Ayaan feel about Zainab's one-biscuit idea?
qa.a: Ayaan might feel hurt and left out, since eating raisins at a festival hardly seems a crime to a small cousin.

grounding: A child keeps score of who helped and objects loudly to an unequal split even when receiving the extra.

passage: By Advent, Jana had corrected eleven of Jamal's German essays. She never asked for anything; she just returned them with green ink and a smiley face. His grades went up. And every time he saw green ink, something in his chest tightened. He owed her. On the Friday before the Christmas market opened, Jana asked if he could help carry her grandmother's boxes on Saturday. He had promised his uncle a shift at the bakery. "Sorry, I can't," he said, and watched her smile go small. That night he lay awake doing sums: eleven essays, zero favours. On Monday he brought her a whole bag of his uncle's pastries. Jana looked puzzled. "Jamal, it's not a shop," she said. "You don't have to pay me back."

qa.q: How many essays had Jana corrected by Advent?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Jamal feel after saying he couldn't help on Saturday?
qa.a: He felt guilty and in debt, lying awake counting eleven essays against zero favours returned.

qa.q: What could Jamal do instead of paying Jana back with pastries?
qa.a: He could tell Jana honestly that he felt he owed her and offer help when she really needs it, letting the friendship be give-and-take rather than a ledger.

qa.q: How does Jana see the bag of pastries?
qa.a: Jana is puzzled, since she helped as a friend and never thought of it as a debt.

grounding: A teenager helped repeatedly by a friend feels a pull to repay and guilt when he cannot, turning the friendship into a ledger.

passage: Aditi, since you're moving into a flat, let your Tejas kaka tell you about Room 12. We were four boys in Pune, and one of them, Sandy, was great fun. But he borrowed Nitin's iron, ate Kiran's pickle and asked me for bus money every week, and he never once bought milk. Nobody said anything. We just, slowly, stopped. Nitin began locking the iron in his cupboard. Kiran hid the pickle behind the rice. I started saying "no change" even when I had some. At dinner there were little jokes: "Sandy's treat today? Ha!" Sandy laughed too, but he began eating out alone. Months of this, and not one straight conversation. Finally, just before exams, Kiran said it plainly: "You take, you don't give, and we're tired." Sandy went red. Then he bought milk for a month. It could have been fixed in week one.

qa.q: What did Nitin begin locking in his cupboard?
qa.a: His iron.

qa.q: How did young Tejas feel about Sandy, judging by the "no change" excuse?
qa.a: He felt quietly resentful and tired of being used, but uncomfortable confronting Sandy, so he pulled back with a small lie.

qa.q: What choice in the story finally changed things, and why?
qa.a: Kiran said plainly, "You take, you don't give, and we're tired," and that direct comment gave Sandy a clear chance to change.

qa.q: What might the dinner jokes have felt like for Sandy?
qa.a: They likely stung and confused him; he laughed along but began eating out alone, sensing he was being pushed out without being told why.

grounding: Flatmates notice one friend keeps taking without giving and quietly withdraw and joke about it for months before anyone confronts him.

passage: Kavitha, you'll be asked for favours all the time here, so let me tell you about my first job. I was twenty-four, a skinny boy called Sumit from Nagpur with a good head for spreadsheets. I helped everyone: fixed formulas, stayed late to check reports, never kept count. Most people helped back one day or another; Farooq brought me biryani the night my father was in hospital. But one colleague, Rakesh, came every Friday at six with "just one small thing", and it was always his whole report. For months I said yes. Then one Friday I heard him tell the boss he had "worked all night" on it. On Monday I told him calmly, "I'll help when you're stuck, Rakesh. I won't do your work any more." He sulked for a week. I kept helping everyone else, just as before. Generous doesn't mean blind, Kavitha.

qa.q: When did Rakesh come with "just one small thing"?
qa.a: Every Friday at six.

qa.q: How did young Sumit feel when he heard Rakesh tell the boss he had worked all night?
qa.a: He felt used and angry, seeing that his generosity had turned into Rakesh's credit.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows mature giving?
qa.a: Sumit calmly told Rakesh he would help when he was stuck but would not do his work, while going on helping everyone else.

qa.q: How might Rakesh have felt after Sumit's words on Monday?
qa.a: Rakesh probably felt embarrassed and put out, sulking for a week because his easy Friday help had ended.

grounding: A young professional helps colleagues generously without counting, but calmly stops doing the work of one who habitually takes.

passage:
"Can I be the reindeer?" Thomas held up the tinsel antlers from the colony Christmas party box.
"No," said Pooja. "You can't play with us. Only big kids."
"I'm five."
"Still no."
Thomas stood very still by the tree, antlers in his hand.
Later Mummy found him on a bench. "Thomas? Why aren't you playing?"
"My tummy hurts." He pressed the middle of his chest. "Pooja said I can't play."
Mummy pulled him onto her lap. "That hurts, na? Being left out really hurts."
"Can we make our own reindeer game?"
"Yes. You be the reindeer, and I'll be the sleigh."

qa.q: What did Thomas hold up from the party box?
qa.a: The tinsel antlers.

qa.q: Why does Thomas say his tummy hurts?
qa.a: He feels hurt and sad after Pooja left him out, and the pain of being excluded shows up as a tummy ache.

qa.q: What does Mummy get right?
qa.a: She takes his pain seriously, says that being left out hurts, and helps him find a new game instead of brushing it off.

qa.q: Why might Pooja say only big kids can play?
qa.a: Pooja may want to feel grown up and in charge of the game, not realising how much the words hurt Thomas.

grounding: A young child told he can't play freezes and says his tummy hurts, showing that exclusion feels like real pain.

passage: After the summer holidays, Parul came back to Class 5 with a new pencil box and a story about the mountains. But on Monday, Rafiq and the others at her table turned their heads away when she spoke. On Tuesday they passed a note right over her desk, as if she were air. Nobody said why. Nobody teased her; that might have been easier. Parul went over the last week of the holidays again and again. Had she forgotten a birthday? Said something wrong in the group call? At lunch she ate her paratha very slowly. That evening Mummy found her on the stairs, still in uniform. "They're not angry," Parul whispered. "They're just not seeing me." Mummy sat down beside her and listened until it was all out.

qa.q: What did Parul bring back after the summer holidays?
qa.a: A new pencil box and a story about the mountains.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when her friends passed the note over her desk?
qa.a: She felt invisible, anxious and confused, replaying the holidays to work out what she might have done.

qa.q: What could Mummy and Parul do next?
qa.a: They could talk it through calmly and, if it goes on, tell the class teacher, who can gently find out what has gone wrong without blaming Parul.

qa.q: What would change if Rafiq told Parul what was wrong?
qa.a: Parul could understand and perhaps fix it, instead of being stuck in a silent confusion that hurts more than teasing.

grounding: A child whose friends stop speaking to her feels invisible, anxious and confused, finding the silence worse than teasing.

passage: At the summer cricket camp, Chetan had a rule for the boys in his batch: nobody sits with Pradeep. "He's a show-off. He bowled me out on purpose," Chetan said, though everyone knew bowling people out was the whole point. Soon the lunch bench had a gap at one end, where Pradeep ate alone. Chetan liked how the others looked at him before deciding where to sit. It felt like being captain. But at night he thought about last year at his old school, when he was the one eating alone. If Pradeep got popular, Chetan might end up there again. So on Thursday, when Pradeep waved at him, Chetan turned away quickly, before anyone could see him wave back.

qa.q: Why did Chetan say Pradeep was a show-off?
qa.a: Because Pradeep bowled him out on purpose.

qa.q: What is Chetan afraid of at night?
qa.a: He is afraid that if Pradeep becomes popular, he will end up eating alone again, as he did at his old school.

qa.q: How could a coach at the camp break up the freeze-out?
qa.a: The coach could mix lunch groups and practice pairs, speak privately with Chetan about the rule, and check in kindly with Pradeep.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep on the lunch bench?
qa.a: It is lonely and confusing to eat alone at the end of the bench, shut out for playing well.

grounding: A boy who organises his batch to shun a classmate feels powerful and safe, acting from fear of being left out again himself.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9C, Friday
For two weeks I have noticed Uday eating lunch alone on the steps behind the science block. His friends from last year sit in the canteen. On Wednesday, when I asked the class to check the project details in the class group, Uday said quietly that he wasn't in it any more. He said nothing else, and I didn't press; I didn't want to make a scene. Today I paired him with Nishant and Ishani for the model-making task, both kind and busy students, and put Uday in charge of the circuit, since his wiring was the best in the lab test. By the end of the period the three were arguing happily over a battery. I have added Uday back to the class group myself and will keep an eye on lunchtime.
Tenzin, class teacher

qa.q: Where had Uday been eating lunch?
qa.a: On the steps behind the science block.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin choose not to press Uday for more?
qa.a: Tenzin felt concerned but careful, not wanting to embarrass Uday by turning his loneliness into a scene in front of the class.

qa.q: Why was pairing Uday for the model task a wise step?
qa.a: It included him naturally, with kind classmates and a role using his best skill, breaking the isolation without drawing attention.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Uday to say he wasn't in the group any more?
qa.a: It was probably embarrassing and lonely to admit in front of the class that he had been dropped.

grounding: A teacher notices a student eating alone and dropped from the class group, and quietly includes him in a task where he shines.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, Vinita's roommate in second year, so I saw most of it. In October her old gang from first year made a new group and simply left her out: the trips, the birthday dinners, all of it turned up in photos she wasn't in. For a few nights she was very quiet, and once I heard her crying on a call with her sister. I don't know everything she felt. But she told me plainly, "It hurts, and I don't know what I did." She didn't post anything nasty. She didn't start a rival group. Instead she joined the Sunday trekking club, started eating dinner with the girls from the third floor, and kept texting the two old friends who still replied. By December she was laughing again. Once she said, "Maybe we just grew apart. It doesn't mean I'm the problem."

qa.q: Which club did Vinita join?
qa.a: The Sunday trekking club.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi think Vinita felt, and why?
qa.a: Vinita was very quiet for nights, cried on a call with her sister and said plainly that it hurt, though Jahnavi cannot know everything she felt.

qa.q: Which of Vinita's choices helped her recover?
qa.a: Admitting the hurt, joining the trekking club, making new dinner friends and staying in touch with those who replied, while refusing to retaliate.

qa.q: How might the old gang see Vinita now?
qa.a: They may barely notice, or be surprised she moved on without bitterness, since she never posted anything nasty or formed a rival group.

grounding: A roommate watches a young woman shut out by her old friends admit the hurt, find new people and refuse to exclude anyone in return.
